''Strain produced by Bending''.—The strain produced stress in a bar or beam is, as regards any imaginary fila along the length of the piece, sensibly the same as if that filament were directly pulled or compressed by itself. The resulting deformation of the piece consists, in the first place and chiefly, of curvature in the direction of the length, due to the longitudinal extension and compression of the filaments, and, in the second place, of transverse flexure, due to the lateral compression and extension which go along with the longitudinal extension and compression. Let <math>l_1</math> (fig. 35) be a short portion of the length of a beam strained by a bending moment <math>\text{M}</math> (within the limits of elasticity). The beam, which we assume to be originally straight, bends in the direction of its length to a curve of radius <math>\text{R}</math>, such that <math>\text{R}/l=y_1/\delta l</math>, <math>\delta l</math> being the change of <math>l</math> by extension or compression at a distance <math>y_1</math> from the neutral axis. But <math>\delta l=lp_1/\text{E}</math>, and <math>p_1=\text{M}y_1/\text{I}</math>. Hence <math>\text{R}=\text{EI}/\text{M}</math>. The transverse flexure is not, in general, of practical importance. The centre of curvature for it is on the opposite side from the centre for longitudinal flexure, and the radius is <math>\text{R}\sigma</math>, where <math>\sigma</math> is the ratio of longitudinal extension to lateral contraction under simple pull.
